# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

[step 444] AGENT Here's how the quick action menu works:

**Opening:** Long-press on focused card → glass overlay appears with grouped actions + control hints

**When menu is open, volume buttons are repurposed:**
- **Volume-down single** → cycles through actions (with haptic selection feedback)
- **Volume-down double** → cancels/dismisses menu
- **Volume-up** → confirms and executes selected action (with haptic)
- **Tap dimmed background** → also cancels

**When menu is closed**, volume buttons work normally (cycle surfaces, cycle workspaces, speech toggle).

**Actions available:**
- Input: Enter, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+D, Ctrl+Z, Clear
- Terminal: Split Pane (Cmd+D), Split Horizontal (Cmd+Shift+D), New Tab (Cmd+T), Close Pane (Cmd+W)
- Workspace: New Workspace

The selected action is highlighted with a brighter background. Each action also has a tap target so you can tap directly too. After executing, surfaces auto-refresh after 0.5s to pick up new panes/tabs.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Plan Review Loop

After completing each chunk of the plan:

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.
   - Provide: chunk content, path to spec document
2. If ❌ Issues Found:
   - Fix the issues in the chunk
   - Re-dispatch reviewer for that chunk
   - Repeat until ✅ Approved
3. If ✅ Approved: proceed to next chunk (or execution handoff if last chunk)

**Chunk boundaries:** Use `## Chunk N: <name>` headings to delimit chunks. Each chunk should be ≤1000 lines and logically self-contained.

**Review loop guidance:**
- Same agent that wrote the plan fixes it (preserves context)
- If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance
- Reviewers are advisory - explain disagreements if you believe feedback is incorrect

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Ready to execute?"**

**Execution path depends on harness capabilities:**

**If harness has subagents (Claude Code, etc.):**
- **REQUIRED:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Do NOT offer a choice - subagent-driven is the standard approach
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If harness does NOT have subagents:**
- Execute plan in current session using superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

Reuse: rekursiver CTE auf `facts`-Tabelle (siehe `team-briefing-technical.md` § Graph).\n6. `POST /api/admin/reingest` — triggert `needs_refresh=true` für SourceRecord(s) → lazy re-derivation pickt das auf. Reuse: existing flag in `source_records` (Migration 007).\n7. `GET /api/admin/pending-types` + `POST /api/admin/pending-types/{id}/decide` — Inbox für autonome Ontologie-Vorschläge. Erfordert neue Tabelle `pending_types`.\n\n**Auth & Schutz**\n8. **JWT-Middleware** für `/api/*` (Supabase JWT, HS256 mit `JWT_SECRET`, oder JWKS bei späteren Deploys). Dev-Bypass über `API_AUTH_DISABLED=true` in `.env`. Implementiert als `Depends(get_principal)` und auf Router-Ebene. Mehrere Levels: `read` (default), `write` (POST/PATCH), `admin` (`/admin/*`).\n9. **MCP-Token-Auth**: neue Tabelle `agent_tokens (id, name, token_hash, scopes text[], created_at, last_seen_at, revoked_at)`. Tokens werden via `cli.py` neu generiert (`uv run server token issue --scopes read,write`).\n10. **Rate Limiting** mit `slowapi`: per-IP default `60/min`, per-Token `600/min`, per-API-Key konfigurierbar. Mounted als FastAPI-Middleware + `@limiter.limit` decorators an heißen Endpoints (`/api/search`, `/mcp/*`).\n\n**Pagination**\n11. **Cursor-Pagination** auf `list_recent_changes`, `/api/changes/recent`, `/api/search`, `/api/admin/pending-types`. Schema: opaque base64-cursor `{last_id, last_ts}`. Helper in neuem `server/api/_pagination.py`. Neue Tabelle `webhooks (id, url, secret, event_types text[], created_by, created_at, active)` und `webhook_deliveries (id, webhook_id, event_id, status, attempts, last_error, delivered_at)`.\n13. ### Performance impact
Before: FilePointer resolution blocked the FUSE thread for O(N * 10s) per folder during metadata refresh. With 10 files, a single `drain_refresh_completions()` call could block for up to 100 seconds.

The `git diff --quiet` check catches the scenario where `pnpm api:generate` WAS run but the dev forgot to stage the output. CodeRabbit's concern — "what if api:generate was never run?" — is an inherent limitation: if the command was never executed, the generated file on disk is unchanged, and no git-level check can detect that without actually running the generation (which would be too slow for a pre-commit hook).

Body read twice when CheckResponse precedes DecodeJSON

2. **`trail create`** — `POST /api/v1/trails/:org/:repo`
   - Currently: local `store.Write()` + push branch + push trails branch

### Phase 2: Add new commands matching API capabilities

5. **`trail delete`** — `DELETE /api/v1/trails/:org/:repo/:trailId`

## Critical scope clarification (read before writing any code)

We cannot know what a model that did NOT actually serve a task would have 
produced — there is no live LLM access, so no counterfactual response can 
ever be generated. This means:
- We CAN heuristically score the actual response of the model that really 
  served each task (from the log).
- We CANNOT score what our router's suggested model would have produced 
  for that same task, because that response never existed and never will 
  in this project.
- The only way to get evidence about "would a cheaper model have done 
  fine here" is a BUCKET-LEVEL comparison: group tasks by estimated 
  difficulty, then compare average quality (heuristic) of tasks that 
  HAPPENED to be served by cheap models vs. tasks that HAPPENED to be 
  served by expensive models, within the same bucket. This is a 
  statistical/aggregate claim about a difficulty tier, not a per-task 
  guarantee, and it depends entirely on our difficulty buckets actually 
  capturing what makes a task hard. Every function/output related to this 
  must make this scope explicit in docstrings and printed summaries, so 
  we don't accidentally overclaim in the presentation.

   clarify", "as an AI", etc. — configurable keyword list)

   complexity (bottom decile within complexity bucket, reuse complexity 
   features from feature_extraction.py via import) OR looks truncated 
   (no terminal punctuation, cuts mid-word)
3. tool_skip_penalty — task had stakes-tools available (reuse 
   tool_surface_stakes from feature_extraction.py) but no evidence any 
   tool was called before the final response
4. unresolved_error_penalty — most recent tool result was an error/failure

5. repetition_penalty — near-duplicate repeated phrases/sentences in the

## Context

I have a dataset of real AI-agent LLM call logs, exported as chunked JSONL files 
(e.g. export/trajectories_v1_01.jsonl, trajectories_v1_02.jsonl, ...). Each line 
is ONE LLM call, in OpenAI-compatible Responses format, with exactly three fields:

- "model": string id of the model that served this call (~9 possible ids across 
  families like claude-opus-*, claude-sonnet-*, claude-fable-*, gpt-5.6-*)
- "input": a list of items representing the FULL growing conversation history up 
  to this call — items can have type "message" (role: system/user/assistant), 
  "function_call", "function_call_output", or reasoning items. Each call's input 
  contains every item from every prior call in that same task.
- "tools": list of tool/function definitions available to this call (e.g. bash, 
  wait_for_background_work, send_email-type tools, etc.)

There is NO output field for the final call of a task, no usage/token counts, and 
no trajectory/task id — tasks must be reconstructed by grouping calls that share 
the same opening messages and ordering by input length (shorter input = earlier 
call in the same task).

## Step 1: Data loader + trajectory reconstruction

Write a script `load_trajectories.py` that:
- Reads all trajectories_v1_*.jsonl files from a given export/ directory
- Parses each line as a call record
- Groups calls into trajectories: calls whose "input" list shares an identical 
  prefix (same system message + same first user message) belong to the same 
  trajectory
- Within a trajectory, orders calls by input length ascending (fewer input items 
  = earlier call)
- Outputs a list of trajectory objects, each containing an ordered list of its 
  calls, and print summary stats (number of trajectories found, calls per 
  trajectory distribution, distinct model ids seen)

## Step 2: Feature extraction per call

Write `feature_extraction.py` that, given a trajectory (ordered list of calls), 
computes the following features for EACH call in the trajectory:

1. **position**: integer index of this call within the trajectory (0-based), 
   plus position as a fraction of estimated remaining trajectory length if 
   inferable
2. **cumulative_input_tokens_est**: estimate of total prefix size in tokens, 
   using a simple chars/4 heuristic over the serialized input, clearly labeled 
   as an estimate
3. **input_delta_tokens_est**: token estimate of ONLY the new items added since 
   the previous call in this trajectory (i.e., input_len(call_i) - 
   input_len(call_i-1))
4. **tool_surface_count**: number of tools available to this call
5. **tool_surface_stakes**: boolean/flag for whether the toolset includes any 
   tool that looks irreversible or externally-visible (e.g. name contains 
   "send", "post", "pay", "delete", "approve", "publish", "email", "message" — 
   build this as a configurable keyword list I can edit)
6. **reasoning_present**: boolean, true if ANY reasoning-type item appears 
   anywhere earlier in this trajectory's input history
7. **failure_flag**: boolean, true if the immediately preceding 
   function_call_output in the input looks like an error (look for keywords 
   like "error", "exception", "failed", "traceback" in the output content, or a 
   structured error field if present)
8. **retry_loop_flag**: boolean, true if the same tool name appears called 2+ 
   times in a row with similar arguments in the recent history (simple 
   similarity: same tool name + high string overlap in arguments)
9. **phase_change_signal**: a small struct/dict capturing:
   - tool_call_density_trend: ratio of function_call items to message items in 
     the last N=3 calls vs the trajectory average
   - last_item_type: whether the input's last item before this call was a 
     function_call_output (suggesting this call likely continues tool 
     execution) or a message (suggesting this call likely produces a 
     user-facing response)
   - resumed_from_wait: boolean, true if the immediately preceding item is a 
     function_call_output for a "wait_for_background_work"-style tool (checkpoint 
     signal)
10. **opening_task_keywords**: (computed once per trajectory, at call_1, then 
    copied to all calls) — extract the first user message text and flag presence 
    of keyword buckets I'll configure, e.g. ["quick", "draft", "check"] vs 
    ["analyze", "decide", "approve", "critical"]

Output this as one row per call (e.g. a pandas DataFrame or list of dicts), 
with trajectory_id, call_index, and all features above, plus the actual "model" 
that was logged (kept aside as ground truth, NOT used as a feature).

## Step 3: Cache-aware switch-cost gate

Write `switch_gate.py` implementing:

```python
def switch_worth_it(prefix_tokens_est, remaining_calls_est, 
                     remaining_tokens_est, rate_old, rate_new):
    """
    Returns True if switching models NOW is worth the one-time cost of 
    re-pricing the full prefix at the new model's uncached rate, given the 
    projected savings over the rest of the trajectory.
    
    reprice_cost = prefix_tokens_est * rate_new
    future_savings = remaining_tokens_est * (rate_old - rate_new)
    return future_savings > reprice_cost
    """
```
Also implement a simpler baseline variant `switch_worth_it_simple(prefix_tokens_est, 
threshold)` that just checks if prefix_tokens_est is below a configurable 
threshold — for comparison purposes.

Note: since we don't know remaining_calls_est/remaining_tokens_est in a live 
setting, implement a reasonable estimator using average trajectory length seen 
in the dataset so far, and let me override it with a parameter.

## Step 4: Rule-based router

Write `baseline_router.py` that ties it together:
- At call_index 0: set a base model tier from opening_task_keywords + 
  tool_surface_stakes
- At every subsequent call: compute an "escalate score" combining 
  failure_flag, retry_loop_flag, reasoning_present, tool_surface_stakes, and 
  phase_change_signal (weighted sum, weights as named constants at the top of 
  the file so I can tune them easily)
- If escalate score crosses a threshold AND switch_worth_it() approves the 
  switch cost → change tier for this call and all subsequent calls (until 
  re-evaluated)
- Otherwise → hold the previously assigned model for this call
- Output: for every call, the assigned model tier, whether a switch happened, 
  and which rule(s) triggered it (for explainability in the presentation)

## Step 5: Baseline comparison stats

Print/save a summary comparing:
- Number of switches your router makes vs. the logged data's implicit 0 
  switches per trajectory (since one model serves all calls in the real log)
- Rough cost estimate (sum of tokens_est * rate per assigned tier) for your 
  router's routing vs. a naive "always cheapest" and "always most expensive" 
  baseline, using placeholder per-tier rates I can edit in a config file

## General requirements
- Python 3, use pandas if helpful, no external API calls, must run on a laptop 
  with no GPU
- Keep all thresholds/weights as named constants at the top of each file, not 
  magic numbers buried in logic
- Add docstrings explaining WHY each feature/rule exists (I need to defend 
  these to a judging panel)
- Ask me for a sample of the actual JSONL data first if you need to see real 
  field names/structure before writing the parser, rather than guessing

[step 33] AGENT Good news and a real gap. Two separate answers depending on whether you're chunking **time** or **ids**.

## Time chunks: already exists — `faucet backfill`

This is exactly "specify the chunk size":

```bash
faucet backfill --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-08-01 --window 1d --concurrency 8
```

```yaml
backfill:
  window: 1d          # 1d / 6h / 30m / 45s / 1w
  concurrency: 8
  timezone: UTC
source:
  type: rest
  config:
    url: "https://api.example/records?updated_from=${backfill.start}&updated_to=${backfill.end}"
```

`plan_windows` (`cli/src/backfill/plan.rs:161`) chunks `[from, to)` into contiguous **half-open** windows of your size, runs them concurrently under a JoinSet, gives each unit its own state key (`{name}::backfill::{unit}`), and keeps a durable progress marker so `--resume` picks up only the unfinished units. Capped at 10,000 units. Also available over HTTP: `POST /v1/backfill`.

Caveat: it's a *bounded historical replay* command, not your everyday incremental run, and the range comes from the CLI, not the bookmark.

## Id/numeric chunks: does not exist

Nothing generates numeric ranges from a chunk size. The pieces that look close aren't reusable as-is:
- `plan_pk_shards` (`crates/core/src/shard.rs:124`) splits an int range — but takes a **target shard count**, not a chunk size, and gets MIN/MAX by querying the database. No API to query for a REST source.
- REST `partitions` is a hand-written `Vec<HashMap<String, Value>>` — static list, no generation.

So what you want is roughly:

```yaml
source:
  type: rest
  config:
    url: "https://api.example/records?id_from={id_from}&id_to={id_to}"
    partition_concurrency: 8
    partition_range:
      from: 0
      to: 1000000
      chunk_size: 10000
      from_param: id_from
      to_param: id_to
      bounds: inclusive        # or half_open
```

Before I build that, three things will bite, and two are correctness issues:

**1. Boundary semantics must be explicit.** Backfill is half-open `[start, end)`. An API with an inclusive `id_to` chunked half-open silently **drops** every boundary record; chunked inclusive against an exclusive API silently **duplicates** them. This has to be a config field with no clever default, not an assumption.

**2. Per-partition bookmarks don't exist.** Today partitions run through `fetch_all` and concatenate, with one replication value for the whole stream. With N concurrent chunks and a failure at chunk 47, there's no per-chunk resume — you either replay everything or, worse, advance a bookmark past chunks that never landed. Chunking amplifies this from "rare" to "routine." Backfill dodges it by giving each unit its own state key; in-run partitions would need the same.

**3. Memory.** Partitioned fetch uses `fetch_all`, **not** `stream_pages` (`crates/source/rest/src/stream.rs:258`). Chunking 1M ids into 100 chunks buffers all 1M records in memory. Fine for a static 3-partition config; not fine once chunk size makes hundreds of partitions the normal case. Partitioned fetch needs to stream before auto-chunking is safe to ship.

**And an open question for you:** where does `to` come from for ids? You usually don't know max id up front. Options are an explicit `to`, or an unbounded final chunk (`plan_pk_shards` does this with `hi_unbounded` so late-arriving rows above MAX aren't lost), or a probe request. Which fits your API?

---

Per the repo's rules this is one feature, not three, and #2/#3 are in-scope edges rather than follow-ups — auto-chunking that can't resume or that OOMs isn't done. My recommendation: file it as one `enhancement`/`tier-2` issue covering range generation + explicit bounds + per-partition state keys + streaming partitioned fetch, then implement it.

## Why the source, not the sink

Cleanup requires a **completeness claim**: "these are *all* the records for scope X." The sink can't make that claim. It sees a page of records and has no way to distinguish "the complete set for contact 123" from "page 1 of 3" from "a partial page before a failure."

The practical argument is the same one: the scope predicate is *already* in your source config (`/contacts/${contacts.id}/associations`). Declaring it again on the sink means writing the same filter twice, and when the two drift you delete the wrong rows. Derive it from the source.

**And the case that clinches it — your exact scenario.** Contact 123 had 5 associations, now has 0. The child fetch returns **zero records**. A sink-side design that infers scopes from the records it saw never learns scope 123 existed, so those 5 stale rows live forever — the precise bug you're trying to fix. Scope declared by the source/invocation comes from the *parent record*, so it survives an empty result set. That's not a detail; a records-derived design is simply wrong for the case you care about.

## Shape

Source asserts completeness; sink opts in to acting on it. Both sides required, so deletes can never happen by accident:

```yaml
matrix:
  - id: associations
    parent: contacts
    source:
      type: rest
      config:
        url: "https://api/contacts/${contacts.id}/associations"
        complete_for:                      # completeness claim
          contact_id: "${contacts.id}"
    sink:
      write_mode: upsert
      key: [association_id]
      cleanup: delete_missing              # opt in
```

Execution stays sink-side (only it can `DELETE`), via a new defaulted trait method — `Sink::cleanup_scope(scope, seen_keys)` — defaulting to unsupported so no existing connector breaks, overridden by the sinks that already do upsert.

## The rule that makes it safe

**Cleanup runs once per invocation, after a fully successful run — never per page.** Two ways to get this wrong, both silent data loss:

- **Per page**: contact 123's associations span two pages → page 2's "delete what I didn't see" wipes what page 1 just wrote.
- **On a failed/partial run**: the fetch died at 40% → "delete what I didn't see" deletes the 60% that simply hadn't arrived. Must be skipped on failure, cancellation, `--limit`, `--dry-run`, and shard runs — the same guard list the SLA and catalog post-run passes already use in `run_one_invocation`.

Two decisions I need from you before filing:

1. **Delete mechanism.** For per-contact scopes (small), simplest and exactly correct is *delete-all-in-scope then write, in one transaction*. For large scopes that's a big delete + rewrite, and the scalable alternative is stamping a run marker column and anti-joining (`DELETE WHERE scope AND _faucet_run <> current`) — but that adds a column to your table. Which fits your associations volume?

2. **Scope column naming.** `complete_for` is written in source terms, but the DELETE runs against destination columns. If a transform renames `contactId` → `contact_id`, a source-declared scope won't match. Do your source field names and destination columns line up, or do you need the scope expressed in destination terms?

Answer those and I'll file it — `feature`/`tier-1`, since silently-retained stale rows is the data-correctness class the repo treats as most severe — and implement it.

Declaring it a second time on the sink means two copies of one predicate; when they drift, the pipeline deletes the wrong rows.\n2. **The empty-result case, which is decisive.** Contact 123 had 5 associations and now has 0. The child fetch returns **zero records**. Any design that infers scopes from the records it saw never learns that scope 123 existed, and the 5 stale rows survive — i.e. it fails precisely the case the feature exists to fix. A scope declared by the source/invocation comes from the parent record and survives an empty result set.\n\n### Config\n\n```yaml\nmatrix:\n  - id: associations\n    parent: contacts\n    source:\n      type: rest\n      config:\n        url: \"https://api/contacts/${contacts.id}/associations\"\n        complete_for:                    # completeness claim\n          contact_id: \"${contacts.id}\"\n    sink:\n      write_mode: upsert\n      key: [association_id]\n      cleanup: delete_missing            # opt in to acting on the claim\n```\n\nBoth sides are required. A source claim with no sink opt-in is inert; a sink opt-in with no source claim is a load-time error. ## What happened

The finding was real and I fixed it correctly — but the commit that carried the fix, `e3610e50`, **also deleted `validateRevision` and all three of its call sites**, reverting this PR's entire change. I pushed that. It was on the remote for about two minutes.

**The cause.** Earlier, to test whether the tests still discriminate, I ran:

```
cp -R "$SP/pr133-merge" "$SP/p133-final-nofix"
cd "$SP/p133-final-nofix" && git checkout 2bced5fc -- internal/cli/root.go
```

A `cp -R` of a git worktree copies the `.git` *file*, which is a pointer to the shared admin directory `.git/worktrees/pr133-merge` — including its **index**. So `git checkout ... -- root.go` inside the "copy" wrote the reverted file into the copy's working tree *and* staged the reverted blob in the original worktree's index. `pr133-merge` was then in a split state: working tree had the fix, index did not.

Then `git add root_test.go && git commit` committed the index — reverted `root.go` included.

**Why my gate didn't catch it.** `go test` reads the *working tree*, which still had the fix, so `internal/cli` passed while the index was already poisoned. Every check I ran was green against a state that wasn't what I was committing. I also read `2 files changed, 8 insertions(+), 42 deletions(-)` in the commit output and only questioned it after the push had gone out.

## The fix

`c525deb9` restores `internal/cli/root.go` byte-identical to `83028875`. Before committing I verified the *staged blob* rather than the working tree — `git show :internal/cli/root.go` confirmed 1 definition and 4 references of `validateRevision`. Net branch diff vs main is back to `root.go +38` / `root_test.go +123`.

Two things, both applicable beyond this repo:

2. **Read the commit stat and verify staged content, not working-tree content**, whenever a commit is going to be pushed. The stat line told me something was wrong and I moved past it.

[step 165] ACTION Bash: gh pr create --title "fix(strategy): hint on gated pre-push when checkpoints are waiting" --body "## Problem

Since the single-remote gate (ENT-1451, shipped in v0.10.0), a push to a non-elected remote silently stops carrying checkpoints. A user whose habitual push remote loses the default election to a dormant \`origin\` sees checkpoints strand locally with **no signal in the push output** — the skip only shows in \`entire status\` and the debug log. The first real user hit this within a day of the release (\"I have a bunch of repos where the git remote I push to isn't called origin. It looks like this means I no longer push checkpoints. Is that intentional?\").

## Change

The pre-push hook prints a two-line stderr hint on a gated push:

\`\`\`
[entire] 3 checkpoint(s) are waiting to sync to \"origin\", this repo's checkpoint sync remote; this push to \"fork\" does not carry them.
[entire] To sync checkpoints to \"fork\" instead, set strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote to \"fork\" in .entire/settings.json.
\`\`\`

It stays quiet when:
- the election was **explicit** (a configured \`checkpoint_push_remote\` is a decision already made — gated pushes are intentional, no nagging),
- the push target is a **raw URL** (the setting takes a remote name; nothing actionable to suggest),
- **nothing is waiting** (a gated push after checkpoints already synced stays clean),
- the **election failed** (the fail-closed path already warns through the gate).

Fully local — reuses \`CountUnpushedCheckpoints\` (push-queue length on git-refs, v1-ahead count on git-branch), no network in the hook.

## Testing

- Unit: \`TestHintGatedCheckpointSync\` covers the hint and all four silence conditions.
- Integration: \`assertSingleRemoteRouting\` now asserts the gated leg's output on both backends — hint present for the default and tracking-config elections, absent for the explicit \`checkpoint_push_remote\` override. New \`RunPrePushOutput\` harness variant captures hook output.
- \`mise run fmt\`, \`mise run lint\` (0 issues), full unit suite (8837 pass), and the \`TestCheckpointSyncRemote\` integration slice all green.

## Non-goals

Whether the election itself should gain a tracking tier (so a habitually-pushed remote can win over a dormant origin without config) stays the product call deferred in #1893/#1951 — this PR only makes the existing gate self-explaining.

# Silent-failure audit: PR #1987 (fix/gated-push-checkpoint-sync-hint)

Scope reviewed: `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go` (`hintGatedCheckpointSync`), its call site in `cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_push.go:85`, and the harness change in `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/testenv.go`.

Structural context that frames every verdict: the hint only runs after `checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote` (checkpoint_sync_remote.go:95-112) has already returned false **and already logged** — `logging.Warn` for a resolution failure (:101), `logging.Debug` with both remote names for the normal mismatch (:106). So `.entire/logs` always carries a record that the gate fired before the hint is even consulted. The question is only whether the hint's own suppression is traceable.

## Findings, ranked

### 1. MEDIUM-HIGH — `CountUnpushedCheckpoints` error is swallowed with zero trace
`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go:133-135`

```go
count, err := CountUnpushedCheckpoints(ctx, syncRemote.Name)
if err != nil || count == 0 {
    return
}
```

This is the one silence in the function that no other code path covers. The `count == 0` half is correct silence (nothing to say). The `err != nil` half is not: `CountUnpushedCheckpoints` (unpushed_checkpoints.go:21) has real, persistent failure modes — on the git-refs backend it can fail at `OpenRepository`, `PushQueueForRepo`, or `queue.Peek()` (a corrupt/locked push queue fails on *every* push); on the git-branch backend `git rev-list` can fail. Hidden error types include repo-open failures (reftable/alternates edge cases), queue-file corruption, and rev-list errors from a broken ref.

User impact: if counting fails persistently, the hint never fires, and the exact symptom this PR exists to fix — checkpoints stranding locally with no signal — reappears. Worse, it reappears *undiagnosably*: the gate's Debug line says "sync skipped" (expected, benign-looking), and nothing anywhere records that the hint was attempted and suppressed by an error. A support engineer reading `.entire/logs` six months from now cannot distinguish "hint correctly silent, nothing waiting" from "hint broken, count failing" without reproducing locally. Notably, on the gated path `prePush` returns immediately (manual_commit_push.go:86), so none of the later repo-open warnings (:107) run either — the count failure has no proxy log.

Verdict: **silence not justified.** Silence toward the *user* is right (never degrade a best-effort hint into push noise or a blocked push), but the error must reach `.entire/logs`. Recommend:

```go
count, err := CountUnpushedCheckpoints(ctx, syncRemote.Name)
if err != nil {
    logging.Debug(ctx, "gated checkpoint sync hint suppressed: cannot count unpushed checkpoints",
        slog.String("sync_remote", syncRemote.Name),
        slog.String("error", err.Error()))
    return
}
if count == 0 {
    return
}
```

Debug matches the gate's severity for expected-skip paths; Warn is defensible since a failing count is abnormal, but Debug is the floor. This is a two-line, zero-risk change.

### 2. LOW (justified, with a caveat) — `isConfiguredRemote` failure conflated with "URL push"
`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:126-128`

`isConfiguredRemote` (manual_commit_push.go:241-246) treats *any* `git remote get-url` failure — git binary broken, config unreadable, context cancelled — as "not a configured remote", so a transient git failure silences the hint for a genuinely configured remote, indistinguishably from the intended raw-URL case. However: (a) this is the helper's documented pre-existing contract, used identically at manual_commit_push.go:224; (b) if git subprocesses are failing, the enclosing `git push` is failing too, with far louder symptoms; (c) the gate's Debug line already recorded `push_remote`. Verdict: **justified** — no change required. If finding #1 is fixed, the log gap here becomes negligible.

### 3. Justified — `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote` error swallowed
`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:129-131`

The identical call just failed inside `checkpointSyncAllowedForRemote` microseconds earlier on the same code path and was logged at Warn with the wrapped specifics (:101-102). Logging again in the hint would be a duplicate entry for one event. The only theoretical gap is a race where the gate's call succeeds and the hint's re-read fails (settings file mutated between the two reads within one hook invocation) — negligible. Verdict: **silence justified.** (Optional hardening, not a defect: pass the gate's resolved `CheckpointSyncRemote` into the hint instead of re-resolving, which removes the double-read and this race entirely.)

### 4. Justified — silence on `Source == SyncRemoteSourceConfig` and on `Name == ""`
`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:130`

The config-source suppression is a deliberate, documented, and integration-tested product decision ("a decision already made must not nag" — asserted by `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_ConfigOverride_RoutesToNamedRemote` passing `expectGatedHint: false`), and the gate's Debug log still records the skip with both remote names. The `Name == ""` arm is actually unreachable here — `isConfiguredRemote(pushRemote)` passing means at least one remote exists, so election always returns a name — a harmless defensive check, not a hidden failure. Verdict: **justified.**

### 5. Justified — `Fprintf` return values ignored
`checkpoint_sync_remote.go:137-142`

Writes go to `stderrWriter` (`os.Stderr` in production, manual_commit_hooks.go:821), inside a git hook where stderr is relayed by git. If the write fails (EPIPE), there is no remaining channel to report on and nothing actionable. This matches every existing user-facing warning in the package (checkpoint_policy.go:60, refs_push_destination.go:114-116). Verdict: **justified.**

### 6. Clean — testenv.go harness change
`cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/testenv.go:1983-2015`

No error path was lost: `runPrePush` still logs combined output via `T.Logf` on **all** paths (:2010) before returning, still wraps the exec error (:2012), and now also returns the output alongside the error (useful, not lossy). `RunPrePush` still `Fatalf`s through `RunPrePushWithError`; the new `RunPrePushOutput` correctly `Fatalf`s on error rather than returning partial output as if it were a clean run — the important trap, and it was avoided. `RunPrePushWithError` discards the output string, but callers doing error-path assertions still get it in the test log. Verdict: **no issues.**

### 7. Observation (pre-existing, not this PR's defect) — the fail-closed misconfiguration remains user-silent at push time

A typo'd `checkpoint_push_remote` disables checkpoint sync on *every* push with no stderr signal; the hint's comment claims the case "warns through the gate itself", but the gate's warning goes to `.entire/logs`, not the user. This is an accepted design: status.go:281-283 explicitly designates `entire status` as the user's signal for this case (`checkpointSyncInfo.Err`), and the resolver's error message is self-explanatory when found. Worth knowing when triaging "my checkpoints stopped syncing" reports; not a regression here.

- **Sole-remote topology**: No test needed. The hint is only invoked inside the gated branch of `prePush` (`manual_commit_push.go:84-87`), and a gated push to a *configured* remote requires ≥2 remotes; with one remote, a gated push can only be a raw URL, which the raw-URL subtest already covers. - **push_sessions disabled**: Gap (see below). Silence is guaranteed only by the `ps.pushDisabled` early return sitting above the gate; nothing asserts it.
- **checkpoint_remote exemption**: Gap (see below). None at the 8-10 level. The feature is a stderr hint; the worst failure modes are wrong or nagging advice, not data loss.

## Important Improvements

**1. Dedicated checkpoint_remote exemption must stay hint-silent — rating 6.**
The gate comment at `manual_commit_push.go:78-84` already warns that hoisting above `resolvePushSettings` breaks the `hasCheckpointURL` exemption; the hint call inherits that exact hazard. The origin tracking ref is absent in that mode, so `CountUnpushedCheckpoints` would return >0 and the hint would fire. Cheapest fix, extending an existing test per house rules: in `TestCheckpointSyncRemote_DedicatedCheckpointRemoteExemptFromGate`, change `env.RunPrePush("publish")` to `RunPrePushOutput` and assert the output does not contain `checkpoint_push_remote`.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step — if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching fresh subagent per task, with two-stage review after each: spec compliance review first, then code quality review.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review (spec then quality) = high quality, fast iteration

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture, design, and review tasks**: use the most capable available model.

**Task complexity signals:**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Proceed to spec compliance review.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- No file reading overhead (controller provides full text)
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Two-stage review: spec compliance, then code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + 2 reviewers per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip reviews (spec compliance OR code quality)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make subagent read plan file (provide full text instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (spec reviewer found issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- **Start code quality review before spec compliance is ✅** (wrong order)
- Move to next task while either review has open issues

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

[step 287] RESULT # uvのMinimum Release Age設定方法

## CLIでの使用方法

コマンドラインで直接指定する場合：

```bash
uv add --exclude-newer "7 days" litellm
uv sync --exclude-newer "7 days"
```

## pyproject.tomlでの設定

設定ファイルに記述する場合は`[tool.uv]`セクションを使用します：

```toml
[tool.uv]
exclude-newer = "1 week"
exclude-newer-package = { tqdm = "2022-04-04T00:00:00Z" }
```

## パラメータの説明

- **`exclude-newer`**：全パッケージに対して相対時間で制限を指定（例：「1 week」「7 days」）
- **`exclude-newer-package`**：特定パッケージのみに絶対時間で制限を指定（ISO 8601形式）

この機能により「公開から一定日数が経過したパッケージのみをインストール」することで、セキュリティ侵害や不安定なリリースのリスクを軽減できます。
